title: Reaction kinetics
overview: Determine rate equations and orders of reaction from experimental data, and link mechanisms and catalysis to kinetics in more depth. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Determine rate equations, orders and k from data.
Use concentration–time and initial-rate evidence, including half-life.
Relate a rate equation to a proposed mechanism and rate-determining step.
Use Arrhenius relationships and explain homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis.

definitions.definition: The exponent of a reactant concentration in an experimentally determined rate equation.
k, the proportionality constant in the rate equation at a fixed temperature.
Time for a reactant concentration to fall to half its value.
The slow elementary step controlling the observed rate.
The minimum energy barrier along a reaction pathway.
A substance that increases rate by providing a lower-activation-energy route and is regenerated overall.

sections.title: Rate equations from data
content: For rate=k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, compare experiments where one concentration changes and others stay constant. A doubled concentration causing unchanged, doubled or quadrupled rate indicates order 0, 1 or 2 respectively. Calculate k after finding all orders and derive its units from the overall order.
bullets: Order is experimental and need not match equation coefficients.
Use initial rates to avoid changing concentrations during the run.

sections.title: Concentration–time evidence
content: A zero-order graph [A] against t is linear; first-order gives constant half-life and ln[A] against t linear; second-order gives increasing half-life and 1/[A] against t linear. Gradient information can determine k where required.
bullets: Constant half-life is strong first-order evidence.
Initial tangent gradients give initial rates.

sections.title: Mechanisms
content: A proposed elementary mechanism must sum to the overall equation and reproduce the observed rate equation. Species in the slow step may determine rate; if an intermediate appears, use a preceding fast equilibrium or step relationship as directed to eliminate it.
bullets: A catalyst may appear in the mechanism but cancels from the overall equation.
Reject a mechanism that conflicts with experimental orders.

sections.title: Temperature and catalysis
content: Arrhenius gives ln k=ln A−Ea/(RT), so a plot of ln k against 1/T has gradient −Ea/R. A homogeneous catalyst shares a phase and may form intermediates; a heterogeneous catalyst adsorbs reactants, weakens bonds, allows reaction, then desorbs products.
bullets: Use kelvin and Ea in J mol⁻¹ with R=8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Catalysts change rate, not ΔH or equilibrium position.

examTips: Show the concentration ratio and rate ratio when deducing each order.
Derive k units from the displayed rate equation rather than memorising.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Copying equation coefficients into a rate equation.
Saying a catalyst makes an equilibrium yield larger.

quickRecall.question: Does stoichiometry determine reaction order?
quickRecall.answer: No; order is found experimentally unless an elementary step is explicitly considered.

quickRecall.question: What kinetic feature indicates first order?
quickRecall.answer: A constant half-life as concentration decreases.

quickRecall.question: What must a valid mechanism reproduce?
quickRecall.answer: Both the overall equation and the experimental rate equation.

quickRecall.question: What does a catalyst change thermodynamically?
quickRecall.answer: It changes neither ΔH nor equilibrium position; it lowers the activation barrier for both directions.
